title: System design framework and estimation
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: The system design interview framework: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive and trade-offs, with back-of-envelope QPS, storage, bandwidth, cache sizing, powers of two and latency numbers.
source: Jeff Dean latency numbers (Designs, Lessons and Advice; Colin Scott interactive version); Hello Interview and ByteByteGo frameworks; Google SRE book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications

questions.prompt: You are asked to "design a photo-sharing service" in a 45 minute interview. What is the best first move?

options.text: Clarify the requirements and expected scale
options.why: Right: scope and numbers decide every later choice.

options.text: Draw the database schema with every column
options.why: Details without scope are likely wasted effort.

options.text: Choose Kafka, Redis and Cassandra first so the design looks current
options.why: Naming technologies before requirements is a classic red flag.

options.text: Start coding the upload endpoint to show depth
options.why: A system design round is not a coding round.

questions.explanation: Typical order: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs and failure modes.

questions.prompt: Match each step of the design framework to the artefact it produces.

right.text: In-scope features, latency and availability targets
Endpoints or RPCs with request and response shapes
Tables or collections, keys and indexes
Detailed treatment of the riskiest component, such as hot keys or cache invalidation
A list of the team's preferred technologies

questions.explanation: Interviewers score structure, so say out loud which step you are on and when you move to the next.

questions.prompt: A service receives 8.64 million requests per day, evenly spread. What is the average number of requests per second?
questions.explanation: 8,640,000 / 86,400 = 100. Quick rule: 1 million per day is about 12 QPS.

questions.prompt: A service stores 100 million new records per day, each 1 KB (1,000 bytes). Data is kept for 365 days and replicated 3 times. How many decimal terabytes of raw storage are needed (one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: 100M x 1 KB = 100 GB per day; x 365 = 36.5 TB; x 3 replicas = 109.5 TB. Add indexes and headroom in a real estimate.

questions.prompt: An API serves 2,000 responses per second, each 50 KB. How many megabits per second of egress bandwidth does it need (1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1,000 bytes)?
questions.explanation: 2,000 x 50 KB = 100 MB/s, and 100 MB/s x 8 = 800 Mbps. That already fills most of a 1 Gbps link, so a CDN is justified.

questions.prompt: A read-heavy service has 50 million reads per day, each returning a 2 KB object, and you decide to cache the hottest 20% of that daily volume. How many decimal gigabytes does the cache need?
questions.explanation: 50M x 2 KB = 100 GB per day; 20% of it is 20 GB, which fits comfortably in one Redis node. This is the 80/20 rule used as an estimate.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Do back-of-envelope estimates before choosing components.
questions.reason: Order-of-magnitude numbers show whether you need sharding, caching or a CDN at all.

whys.a: Right: the reason is the justification.

questions.explanation: A service with 50 QPS and 10 GB of data does not need Cassandra; saying so earns more credit than over-engineering.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: In estimates it is fine to treat a day as roughly 10^5 seconds.
questions.reason: One million requests per day works out to about 12 requests per second.

whys.a: The conversion fact does not justify rounding.
whys.b: Right: both are true; the 12 QPS figure is a consequence of the 10^5 approximation, not the reason it is allowed.

questions.explanation: A day has 86,400 seconds, so 10^5 is within 16%, and the speed gained in mental arithmetic is worth it.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Non-functional requirements such as latency, availability and consistency shape a design.
questions.reason: The CAP theorem says a distributed store can always provide consistency, availability and partition tolerance together.

whys.c: Right: CAP says that during a partition you must give up consistency or availability.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Say which of C or A you choose during a partition for the data in question: payments lean C, a like counter leans A.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: For a read-heavy service the first optimisation to propose is a message queue.
questions.reason: Caches and read replicas absorb read traffic.

whys.d: Right: the assertion is false (queues smooth writes and async work), and the reason names the actual read-side tools.

questions.explanation: Match the tool to the bottleneck: reads need caches, replicas and CDNs; write bursts need queues and batching.

questions.text: 2^10 is about one {1}, 2^20 about one {2}, and 2^30 about one {3}.
questions.explanation: As bytes: 1 KB, 1 MB, 1 GB (decimal approximations of 1,024; 1,048,576; 1,073,741,824). 2^32 is about 4.3 billion, the size of the IPv4 space.

questions.prompt: Reading 1 MB sequentially from main memory is faster than reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD.

options.why: Right: Dean's latency table has roughly 250 microseconds for memory against about 1 ms for SSD per MB.
Memory bandwidth is an order of magnitude beyond an SSD, which is why caches pay off.

questions.explanation: The approximate order: L1 reference 1 ns, main memory 100 ns, SSD random read tens to 150 microseconds, same-datacenter round trip 500 microseconds, disk seek 10 ms.

questions.prompt: A payments ledger needs multi-row transactions, strict uniqueness and ad-hoc reporting. Which store do you defend first?

options.why: Right: ACID transactions, constraints and SQL cover all three needs.

options.text: A wide-column store partitioned by event time bucket
options.why: It gives write scale but weak cross-row transactions.

options.text: An in-memory cache with periodic snapshots
A document store holding one blob per day
options.why: Whole-blob updates make uniqueness and reporting awkward.

questions.explanation: Pick for the access pattern and guarantees, then say what you would change if the load grew 100 times.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in the deep-dive and trade-off phase? Select all that apply.

options.text: Handling a hot key or partition
options.why: Right: a typical scaling risk worth probing.

options.text: Failure modes: node loss, retries, duplicates
options.why: Right: show how the design degrades.

options.text: Asking the interviewer for the expected scale
options.why: That belongs at the start, in requirements.

questions.explanation: Choose one or two components to go deep on, ideally the part with the highest risk or the interviewer's interest.

questions.prompt: Write the SQL to create a table urls for a URL shortener: short_code (VARCHAR(8), primary key), long_url (TEXT, not null) and created_at (timestamp, not null).
questions.explanation: The primary key on short_code gives the index for redirects. Other column orders and types (TIMESTAMPTZ) are fine in practice; the checks here accept TIMESTAMP spelled directly.

questions.prompt: Match each operation to its order-of-magnitude latency from the widely quoted latency table.

left.text: Random 4 KB read from an SSD
Packet round trip California to Netherlands and back

questions.explanation: These are the 2012-era figures attributed to Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig; hardware has moved (NVMe is faster, cross-region RTT is bounded by the speed of light) but the ratios still guide design: memory is thousands of times faster than a network hop, and a cross-continent call costs about 100 ms.

questions.prompt: A service promises 99.9% availability measured over a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime per month does the target allow, rounded to the nearest minute?
questions.explanation: 30 days x 24 h x 60 min = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. Each extra nine divides the budget by ten (99.99% is about 4.3 minutes), which is why the SRE book treats the remaining budget as an error budget.
